text: The idea of secret electronic voting began with Chaum, who showed in 1983 that blind signatures let an authority approve a message without seeing it, which is the basis of anonymous credentials [12]. Nakamoto's Bitcoin paper [1] introduced the blockchain as a way for strangers to agree on a shared record without a trusted party, and Buterin's Ethereum white paper [2] added programmable smart contracts, whose formal definition is given in the Yellow Paper [3]. Overviews of the technology can be found in [4] and [5].

Christidis and Devetsikiotis [6] explained how smart contracts and blockchains can replace intermediaries in many applications, and Kshetri and Voas [14] examined blockchain-enabled voting, noting both its promise for transparency and its open problems of privacy and coercion. Hjalmarsson et al. [13] built a blockchain voting system on a permissioned Ethereum network and showed the benefit of an immutable record, but their design relied on the administrators for identity and scalability was limited.

McCorry, Shahandashti and Hao [16] presented the first implementation of a decentralised, self-tallying voting protocol on Ethereum (the Open Vote Network). It gives strong ballot privacy without trusted tellers, but its running cost grows with the number of voters and it needs an interactive protocol between voters, which is impractical for a general election. Adida's Helios [15] is a web-based, end-to-end verifiable voting system in which ballots are encrypted in the browser and the tally can be audited. It showed the value of public verification, but it keeps its trust in a central server and in a small set of trustees. Park, Specter, Narula, and Rivest [17] argue that internet voting remains hard to secure and that the blockchain alone does not solve the problem of ballot secrecy or of malware on the voter's device. Their warning shapes our choice to keep the prototype to a clearly stated scope.

For the cryptography, RSA [7] with OAEP padding [10] is used to protect a short key, and Galois/Counter Mode [9] provides authenticated encryption of the ballot content. HMAC [11] combined with a hash function from the SHA-3 family [20] (Keccak-256, which is also the hash used inside Ethereum) is used to turn an identity into a voter hash that cannot be reversed without a secret. Shamir's secret sharing [8] splits a key into shares so that any threshold number of them rebuild it and fewer reveal nothing, which is exactly what is needed for a decryption key held jointly by trustees.

text: The main objective is to design, build and test a prototype of a secure, anonymous and verifiable voting system based on blockchain. The specific objectives are:

items: To verify each voter with a one-time password and to represent the voter in the system only by a keyed hash.
To issue each voter one single-use voting token that cannot be traced back to the voter.
To encrypt every ballot in the voter's browser so that all ballots have the same size and no one can read them before the election ends.
To record the ballots in a smart contract that enforces the election phases, the voter limit and one ballot per token.
To place the decryption key under shared control of three trustees, any two of whom can decrypt.
To allow anyone to verify the result by decrypting and recounting with the published key.
To test the system thoroughly and to measure its speed and cost.

text: The project covers the complete life of one election: registration and verification, voting, closing, decryption, tallying and public verification. It is a working prototype that runs on a local test blockchain, and its tooling for a public test network (Sepolia) and for a cloud server is prepared and rehearsed locally.

The following are outside the scope: connection to the real Aadhaar service (the OTP service is a simulation), real SMS delivery, biometric verification, protection against malware on the voter's own device, resistance to coercion in an uncontrolled setting, and a security audit by an independent party. These limits are stated again in the conclusion.

items: India has the largest electorate in the world, and any improvement in the speed, cost and trustworthiness of voting has a very large effect.
Many eligible voters, such as migrant workers, people living abroad, the elderly and people with disabilities, find it difficult to reach a polling booth.
Public confidence in elections is damaged by disputes over counting. A result that anybody can recheck would reduce such disputes.
The team wished to apply the subjects studied in the course, namely communication, networks, security and software, to a problem that matters to society.

text: Although the prototype is described in the language of a government election, the same design applies wherever a trustworthy, secret ballot is needed:

items: student council and university body elections;
elections of cooperative societies, resident welfare associations and trade unions;
shareholder and board voting in companies;
opinion polls and referendums within organisations;
a base for later, larger national or state systems after proper audit.

text: Chapter 1 introduces the problem, the research gap and the engineering attributes. Chapter 2 reviews the literature and states the objectives, scope, motivation and applications. Chapter 3 explains the methodology: existing methods, the proposed method, the architecture and flow, the main components, the workflow, the design constraints and the standards followed. Chapter 4 lists the hardware and software used. Chapter 5 presents the results, the tests and measurements, the impact on society and the mapping to the Sustainable Development Goals. Chapter 6 concludes the report and suggests future work. The references follow.
